entity.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
entity.description: The wine merchant's son who invented English literature. A diplomat, spy, customs inspector, and war prisoner who wrote The Canterbury Tales in his spare time, introducing nearly 2,000 words into the English language. He was the first writer buried in what became Poets' Corner at Westminster Abbey.

story.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
story.description: A vintner's son serves as page, soldier, and spy, gets captured and ransomed during the Hundred Years' War, works as customs inspector by day and poet by night, and writes The Canterbury Tales — legitimizing English as a literary language.

moments.name: Geoffrey Chaucer Is Born to a Prosperous Wine Merchant in London
moments.subtitle: A vintner's son whose family name literally means "shoemaker" in French
moments.description: Around 1343, Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London to John Chaucer, an important wine merchant with royal connections, and Agnes Copton, who inherited 24 shops in London from her uncle. The surname derived from the French "chaucier" (shoemaker), though the family had been vintners for generations. John Chaucer's own childhood had been dramatic — he was kidnapped at age twelve by an aunt trying to marry him off for property. Through his father's connections, young Geoffrey entered the household of Elizabeth de Burgh, Countess of Ulster, as a page around age 14, launching a lifetime career in the orbit of English royalty.

moments.name: Chaucer Is Captured by the French and Ransomed by King Edward III
moments.subtitle: The king pays £16 for a young poet-soldier — equivalent to about £14,000 today
moments.description: In 1360, during the Hundred Years' War, Geoffrey Chaucer was captured by French forces during the siege of Reims while serving in the English army alongside Lionel of Antwerp, Duke of Clarence. King Edward III personally paid £16 for Chaucer's ransom — equivalent to roughly £14,000 today — suggesting the young man was already valued at court. The experience of war and captivity in France exposed Chaucer to French literary culture at a formative age. After his release, Chaucer traveled extensively in France, Spain, and Flanders, encounters that would shape the Continental literary influences evident throughout his later masterworks.

moments.name: Chaucer Becomes Comptroller of Customs for the Port of London
moments.subtitle: By day he polices corrupt tax collectors; by night he writes the greatest English poetry yet composed
moments.description: On 8 June 1374, Geoffrey Chaucer was appointed Comptroller of the Customs for the port of London, a position he held for 12 years. His job was essentially to watch the tax collectors and catch them cheating — while the Exchequer watched Chaucer for the same reason. The same year, Edward III granted Chaucer a gallon of wine daily for life on Saint George's Day, likely rewarding a poetic work. The customs post gave Chaucer financial stability and daily exposure to the cross-section of English society — merchants, pilgrims, sailors, and con artists — that would populate The Canterbury Tales, which he began writing in the early 1380s.

moments.name: Chaucer Travels to Italy and Encounters Petrarch and Boccaccio's Works
moments.subtitle: A customs inspector from London discovers the Italian literary Renaissance firsthand
moments.description: In 1373, Geoffrey Chaucer traveled to Genoa and Florence on a diplomatic mission for the English crown. Scholars believe it was during this and a subsequent 1378 trip to Milan that Chaucer encountered the works of Petrarch and Boccaccio — and possibly met the poets themselves. The Italian literary forms and stories Chaucer absorbed during these visits transformed his writing. Boccaccio's Decameron, a collection of tales told by travelers, likely inspired the frame narrative of The Canterbury Tales. Chaucer's Italian journeys represented the moment when the greatest traditions of Continental literature crossed the English Channel and merged with the English vernacular.

moments.name: Chaucer Is Buried in Westminster Abbey and Founds Poets' Corner
moments.subtitle: The first writer interred there — buried not for his poetry but because he rented a house next door
moments.description: On 25 October 1400, Geoffrey Chaucer died of unknown causes and was buried in Westminster Abbey — the first writer to be interred in what would become known as Poets' Corner. Ironically, Chaucer's burial there had nothing to do with his literary fame: he had leased a house in the abbey close in December 1399 and was buried as a tenant, not as a celebrated poet. His tomb was not erected until 1556, over 150 years later. The Canterbury Tales remained unfinished at his death — only 24 of a planned 120 tales were completed. Despite this, Chaucer's work legitimized English as a literary language at a time when French and Latin dominated.
